title: 5 key takeaways from the F1 drivers' 24h Nürburgring weekend
meta: Published: 18 May 2026 | By Tunde Adebayo, Feature & Human‑Interest Writer | F1CC News
caption: The #160 Porsche of Väisänen, MaraDöner and Thompson running through the night at the Nürburgring.
body:
The Nordschleife does not care who you are. It does not care that you lead the Formula 1 World Championship, or that you are a four‑time world champion returning from a decade away, or that you are a rookie trying to prove you belong anywhere other than the back of an F2 grid. It cares about 73 corners, 300 metres of elevation, and a strip of asphalt that narrows to the width of a country lane in places where the trees lean in close and the barriers have no mercy. Over 24 hours on the weekend of 16–17 May, three cars filled with Formula 1 drivers took on the ADAC Ravenol 24h Race at the Nürburgring. They arrived as F1 stars. They left having learned something about themselves that no grand prix weekend could teach them.

1. Väisänen’s privateer Porsche proved that preparation beats pedigree

The #160 Porsche 911 GT3 R was not a factory effort. It was a privateer entry funded by Eetu Väisänen’s own sponsorship money, crewed by a group of mechanics who had never worked together before this weekend, and driven by three men with almost no shared endurance experience. Yet it finished ninth overall and fourth in the Pro‑Am class, a result that was both a triumph of planning and a vindication of Väisänen’s obsessive approach.

The Ferrari championship leader had spent three months preparing for this race. He chose the Porsche for its tyre management characteristics over a stint. He coached Alex Thompson — the Mercedes junior whose GT3 season had been a study in inconsistency — on exactly how to drive a GT3 car around the Nordschleife. And he gave Michiii MaraDöner a specific set of instructions for the night stint: carry speed through the high‑speed sections, do not overdrive the braking zones, and under no circumstances push before hour seven.

MaraDöner lasted until hour six and forty minutes before the instinct took over. A brush with the wall at Adenauer Forst cost the team thirty‑eight minutes in repairs. But the car came back, and Väisänen’s response — “Good. Now drive the lap, not the corner” — was the calm of a driver who had planned for exactly this eventuality. His own stints were metronomic: two seconds per lap faster than his co‑drivers, eighty‑three minutes of unvarying pace. When asked if Ferrari had any issue with him racing at the Nürburgring, he was brief: “They got to watch their championship leader win in the Eifel. I don’t think they had complaints.”

2. The Audi wagon that should not have existed became the weekend’s most important car

The #67 Audi RS6 Avant GT3 arrived at the Nürburgring as a curiosity. It left as a cult hero. An estate car — a wagon, in the language of the paddock — entered in the experimental SPX class, a category reserved for non‑homologated machinery never intended for conventional GT3 competition. Its only true rival was the #81 Schubert Motorsport BMW M3 Touring, a factory‑backed machine that would go on to finish fifth overall and win the class. The rest of the SPX field — three HWA EVO.Rs and a KTM X‑Bow GTX — were either unclassified or buried deep in the order, none of them true GT3‑style racing cars. The Audi, piloted by a current F1 race winner, a driver still recovering from a back injury, and a four‑time world champion who had not raced competitively since 2018, had no business keeping the BMW honest. It did.

Robin Keisner was the car’s engine. His stints were relentless, his overtaking in multi‑class traffic surgical. He told Lucas Koopman after a close call at Schwedenkreuz — a suspension‑damaging brush with the barrier after an evasive manoeuvre — that the class result no longer mattered. The target was to finish. Koopman drove the remainder of his stints with a discipline that belied his limited experience. And Sebastian Vettel, given the final three laps by his co‑drivers, brought the car home and sat in it for forty seconds without moving. The #67 completed 127 laps, finishing thirty‑first overall and second in the SPX class — the only car other than the Schubert BMW to take the chequered flag in a class designed for machines that were never meant to race at all.

“I forgot what it felt like,” Vettel said. “Not the driving — the driving comes back immediately. I forgot what it felt like when the car stops and you realise you’ve been somewhere for 24 hours and you’re still there.”

Audi’s marketing team issued a three‑sentence press release on Monday morning. It ended with the words “we’ll be back.”

3. Sarah Springfield was the revelation the Aston Martin needed

The #817 Aston Martin Vantage GT3 Evo, running in Red Bull livery, was the product of two F1 teams deciding a shared entry made more sense than arguing over who paid for the tyres. Lukus Wright, the 2024 F1 champion, and Sarah Springfield, Aston Martin’s lead driver, were paired with Linus Lundqvist, the Swedish endurance specialist who provided the GT3 anchor the other two required.

Wright struggled. The Vantage’s characteristic snap oversteer, manageable in warm conditions by a driver who knew the car, became something closer to an event in the cold night hours. He lost four positions in two hours, and admitted afterward that the car had beaten him. “I know how to drive a car,” he said, in the specific way that racing drivers say it when they mean the opposite. “I didn’t know how to drive that car. There’s a difference.”

Springfield was the opposite. She took the car at hour nine in drizzle and within three laps had found two seconds per lap that Wright had been unable to access. Her adaptability — reading wet patches, tyre temperatures through the seat, managing the Vantage’s rear with instinctive throttle modulation — was the quality Lundqvist described as “something you either have or you don’t.” Her four‑hour night stint gained seven positions. The car finished fourteenth overall. “I’ll know how to drive it next time,” she said. If there is a next time, the paddock will be watching more closely.

4. The Nordschleife exposed the difference between being fast and being an endurance driver

Formula 1 drivers are trained to extract maximum performance over a single lap or a short stint. The Nürburgring 24 Hours demands something else entirely: the ability to manage tyres over eighty‑minute runs, to read multi‑class traffic in the dark, to know when to push and when to survive. Not every F1 driver made the transition smoothly.

MaraDöner’s mistake at Adenauer Forst was a classic error of impatience — pushing beyond the limit before the track had cooled enough to make the risk worthwhile. Wright’s struggles with the Vantage in cold conditions revealed that even a world champion’s car control has limits when the car’s behaviour changes beyond the driver’s experience. Koopman’s close call at Schwedenkreuz was a reminder that judging closing speeds in multi‑class traffic is a skill that takes years to develop, not a single test day.

But others thrived. Väisänen’s metronomic consistency was the equal of any factory pro. Keisner’s aggression was applied with just enough precision to keep the Audi out of the barriers. Thompson, the F2 driver who had crashed at Sebring and finished 40th at Long Beach, ran the cleanest stint of the #160’s race in the closing hours. Something about the Nordschleife’s relentlessness, its unwillingness to reward anything but complete commitment in the right places and complete patience in the wrong ones, suited whatever he had been building across his GT3 season.

5. The atmosphere was unlike anything the Nürburgring has seen — and the drivers felt it

The 54th running of the ADAC Ravenol 24h Race was always going to be special, but the presence of seven current F1 drivers — and one returning world champion — elevated the event to something beyond a motorsport competition. Weekend passes sold out for the first time in the event’s history. The campsites around the Nordschleife were packed with fans who had travelled from across Europe, many of them wearing Ferrari, Audi, and Aston Martin merchandise alongside the traditional Nürburgring regalia.

The race was preceded by tragedy — the loss of Juha Miettinen in Thursday qualifying — and the drivers carried that weight through every stint. The minute of silence before the start was observed by 161 cars and a crowd that stretched as far as the eye could see. The shared experience of racing through grief, of pushing through the night with the knowledge that a fellow competitor was not coming home, bound the paddock together in a way that transcended team rivalries.

Vettel’s final stint, the Audi wagon crossing the line with both hands on the wheel, drew a standing ovation that lasted three minutes. Several spectators were crying. Motorsport does this occasionally — produces moments that have nothing to do with winning and everything to do with what the sport is actually about. The F1 drivers who came to the Nürburgring looking for a challenge found something more. They found a community, a test of character, and a reminder that racing, at its core, is not about the size of the audience or the points on a championship table. It is about the car, the track, and the people who stay awake all night to see what happens next.
